{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Lipschitz convex optimization in a general norm with known convex constraints and exact values\par}\vspace{5pt}


\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}ZO\_\allowbreak{}E06cL}



Single-objective optimization



Minimize a globally norm-Lipschitz convex objective over a known convex body using exact scalar values. Matched l1 geometry has an explicit randomized joint dimension-accuracy bracket; other geometries and deterministic regimes retain their own bounds.



\textbf{Status.} Polynomial gap present



\textbf{Gap classes present.} Polynomial gap; Logarithmic gap; Other quantified gap



\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: Global minimization; solution concept: Global minimization; task family: Single objective



\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Convex; smoothness: Function lipschitz in declared norm; structure: No additional structure



\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: Zeroth-order interface; interface family: Exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared; query domain: Full space; operation: Function value; feedback quality: Exact



\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; randomization: Deterministic algorithms; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed



\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required



\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: Objective gap



\textbf{GUARANTEE tags.} aggregation: Per instance; mode: Deterministic; mode: Probability



\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} budget: Fixed worst-case budget



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}


Minimize \AtlasInlineMath{f} globally over \AtlasInlineMath{K} and return a point with small objective gap.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}


\AtlasInlineMath{B\subset\mathbb{R}^d} is a known compact, centrally symmetric convex body with nonempty interior. It induces the norm \AtlasInlineMath{\|x\|_B=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}}. The set \AtlasInlineMath{K\subset\mathbb{R}^d} is known, nonempty, compact and convex.



\AtlasInlineMath{f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}} is globally convex and satisfies \AtlasInlineMath{|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_B}. Constrained minimization is over \AtlasInlineMath{K}; boundary minimizers are allowed.



Ball-geometry subregions are written as \AtlasInlineMath{K=B_p(0,R)} and \AtlasInlineMath{B=B_q(0,1)}. The exponents \AtlasInlineMath{p} and \AtlasInlineMath{q} describe domain geometry and the regularity norm, respectively. General convex-body specifications do not require this ball parameterization.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}


At any finite query point \AtlasInlineMath{x} in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}, the oracle returns the single exact scalar \AtlasInlineMath{f(x)}. The reply is uniquely determined and contains no gradient, subgradient or derivative-vector product.



Projection and the stated proximal operations over known geometry are free.



The public inputs are \AtlasInlineMath{d}, \AtlasInlineMath{B}, \AtlasInlineMath{K}, \AtlasInlineMath{L}, \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}, together with the sets, kernels and auxiliary operations explicitly declared above. Information about the unknown objective and any undisclosed sample distribution is obtained only through the stated interface.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}


Return \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in K}. The output may be an unqueried point, an average or convex combination that remains in the stated space. No function value, gradient, inner solution, or accuracy certificate must accompany the output.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}


The base loss is \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,x)=f(x)-f_*}, where \AtlasInlineMath{f_*=\inf_{u\in K}f(u)}. This nonnegative loss is evaluated at the output, with tolerance \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}


Each scalar function value or noisy observation costs \AtlasInlineMath{1} call. Every location in a multipoint finite difference, every initialization query, and every reference observation is charged.



Only the declared oracle resource is charged. Computation and storage using existing information, together with explicitly known geometric and proximal operations, are free.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic}


Only deterministic strategies are allowed. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.



Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.



After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The requirement \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon} holds deterministically for each instance.



Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized}


Private randomization is allowed, with the seed independent of the instance and external randomness. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.



Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.



After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The error requirement is \AtlasInlineMath{\Pr(\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon)\ge2/3}.



Probability is over the algorithm's random seed only.



Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.



\textbf{Output qualification.} Random selection among previously queried points is permitted, subject to the declared success guarantee.



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{2. Notation and parameters}


\AtlasInlineMath{d}: Dimension of the variable space \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d\in\mathbb{N},\ d\ge1}.



\AtlasInlineMath{B}: Unit ball of the known norm \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{B\subset\mathbb{R}^d}; compact, convex and centrally symmetric, with nonempty interior.



\AtlasInlineMath{\|x\|_B=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}}



\AtlasInlineMath{K}: Known feasible body or minimizer-localization body \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{K\subset\mathbb{R}^d}; nonempty, compact and convex.



\AtlasInlineMath{L}: Public upper bound on the objective Lipschitz constant \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{L>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_B}, \AtlasInlineMath{x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}: Error target; norm and squared-norm criteria use different thresholds \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{a_B}: Comparison coefficient between the specified norm and the Euclidean norm \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{a_B>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{a_B=\max_{\|u\|_2=1}\|u\|_B}



\AtlasInlineMath{R_2(K)}: Radius of the supplied Euclidean enclosing ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{R_2(K)\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{K\subseteq B_2(c_K,R_2(K))}, with known center \AtlasInlineMath{c_K}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{R}}: Combined norm and geometry scale \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{R}\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{R}=a_BR_2(K)}



\AtlasInlineMath{r_m(B,K)}: Radius of the largest Euclidean ball inscribed in the norm-contractive linear image \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{m\in\{1,\ldots,d\},\ r_m(B,K)\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{r_m(B,K)=\sup_{\|P\|_{B\to2}\le1}\sup\{r\ge0:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ z+rB_2(0,1)\subseteq PK\}}; \AtlasInlineMath{P:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^m} is a linear map.



\AtlasInlineMath{m}: Dimension index of the linear image in the hard construction \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{m\in\{1,\ldots,d\}}.



Take the maximum only over integers \AtlasInlineMath{m} satisfying the respective accuracy windows.



\AtlasInlineMath{p}: Norm exponent of the feasible or localization ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{1\le p\le\infty}.



\AtlasInlineMath{q}: Exponent of the regularity norm \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{1\le q\le\infty}.



For ball parameterizations, \AtlasInlineMath{B=B_q(0,1)}; independent of the domain exponent \AtlasInlineMath{p}.



\AtlasInlineMath{R}: Public radius in the explicitly stated feasible-body parameterization \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{R>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{K=B_p(0,R)} in ball-geometry regions, or \AtlasInlineMath{K=c+RB} in matching-body regions.



\AtlasInlineMath{A_B}: Lipschitz accuracy ratio in the matching ellipsoidal subregime \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{A_B>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{A_B=LR/\varepsilon}; used only in the subregime \AtlasInlineMath{K=c+RB}.



\AtlasInlineMath{s}: Proximal-norm exponent chosen by the algorithm \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{1\le s\le\infty}.



Use a public proximal function \AtlasInlineMath{\omega_s} that is \AtlasInlineMath{1}-strongly convex with respect to the \AtlasInlineMath{\ell_s} norm.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Theta_s}: Range of the selected proximal function over the feasible body \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\Theta_s\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Theta_s=\sup_{x\in K}\omega_s(x)-\inf_{x\in K}\omega_s(x)}; \AtlasInlineMath{\omega_s} is known and \AtlasInlineMath{\ell_s}-strongly convex in the \AtlasInlineMath{1} norm.



\AtlasInlineMath{m_0}: Minimum dimension for the linear-image hard construction \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{m_0>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_Z}: Normalized accuracy threshold for the randomized exact-value lower bound \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_Z>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_Z}: Positive multiplicative constant in the randomized exact-value lower bound \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c_Z>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{C}: Upper-bound constant or universal threshold for an applicability window \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{C>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{d_0}: Universal dimension threshold required by the lower bound \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d_0>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{c}: Small positive constant defining the accuracy window \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_1}: Positive constant in the cube accuracy window \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c_1>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_*}: Positive upper-threshold constant for the cube accuracy window \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c_*>0}.



Determined by the applicable theorem conditions; retain a symbolic threshold when no numerical value is supplied.



\AtlasInlineMath{x,y,u}: Function arguments and dummy variables in the formulas \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{x,y,u\in\mathbb{R}^d}; spherical domains are embedded in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}.



Admissible ranges are specified separately by the task, model and oracle in this profile.



\AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}}: Final algorithm output \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{K}.



\AtlasInlineMath{I}: Complete problem instance \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{I\in\mathcal{I}}.



Includes the unknown objective and its admissible feedback distribution or environment law. Public parameters are fixed before the quantifiers.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{I}}: Admissible instance class determined by the eight specification fields in this profile \textbf{Domain:} Instances satisfying the public parameter bounds.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{A}}: Algorithm or strategy \textbf{Domain:} Measurable adaptive strategies allowed in this profile.



The algorithm is selected before the hidden instance.



\AtlasInlineMath{\ell}: Base loss or residual \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\ell:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}}\to[0,+\infty]}.



The exact formula appears in this profile's performance-criterion section.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E},\Pr}: Expectation and probability \textbf{Domain:} Evaluated over the algorithmic and feedback randomness specified by this profile's guarantee.



Fix the instance first; aggregate cost and error separately.



\AtlasInlineMath{\inf,\sup}: Infimum and supremum \textbf{Domain:} Evaluated only over the variable sets explicitly specified in the formula.



In the risk definition, the infimum over algorithms precedes the supremum over instances or centers.



\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}: Euclidean norm and inner product \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y}



\AtlasInlineMath{B_p(c,R)}: Closed norm ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{p\in[1,\infty],\ R\ge0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{B_p(c,R)=\{x:\|x-c\|_p\le R\}}; \AtlasInlineMath{B_2} denotes the Euclidean ball.



\AtlasInlineMath{N,T}: Actual call count and declared budget \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{N,T\in\mathbb{N}_0}.



A fixed budget bounds every execution path; the Markov specification uses an expected budget.



\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde{O}}: Asymptotic upper bounds, lower bounds, matching orders, and upper bounds with hidden logarithms \textbf{Domain:} Within the joint parameter window specified for each complexity regime.



Dependence of hidden constants on fixed parameters is stated separately for each bound. Tilde notation may hide logarithmic factors only in the declared variables.



\AtlasInlineMath{c,C,c_\alpha,C_\alpha}: Positive constant in a proof or asymptotic bound \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c,C,c_\alpha,C_\alpha<\infty}.



Unsubscripted constants have the dependencies stated in the bound; constants subscripted by \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha} may depend only on the fixed smoothness order.



\AtlasInlineMath{\log,\log_+,e}: Natural logarithm, truncated logarithm, and Euler's number \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{z>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\log_+(z)=\max\{0,\log z\}}; \AtlasInlineMath{e=\exp(1)}, and \AtlasInlineMath{\log_2} denotes the base-two logarithm.



\AtlasInlineMath{f,f_*}: Population objective and its optimal value \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{f:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fun}}\to\mathbb{R}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{f_*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_{B,*},\|P\|_{B\to2}}: Dual norm and induced operator norm of a linear map \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{v\in\mathbb{R}^d,\ P:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^m}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\|v\|_{B,*}=\sup_{x\in B}\langle v,x\rangle}, \AtlasInlineMath{\|P\|_{B\to2}=\sup_{x\in B}\|Px\|_2}



\AtlasInlineMath{c_K,c,z}: Known centers of the enclosing ball, affine ellipsoid and inscribed ball in the linear image \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c_K,c\in\mathbb{R}^d,\ z\in\mathbb{R}^m}.



Used only in the corresponding geometric formula.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fun}},\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}},\mathcal{X}}: Function domain, admissible output domain and optimization domain \textbf{Domain:} Each is the Euclidean space or subset explicitly specified in this profile.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}}=K} and \AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}=K}; the function domain is the region on which the model imposes regularity.



\AtlasInlineMath{N^*}: Optimal worst-case oracle complexity satisfying the complete guarantee \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{N^*\in[0,+\infty]}.



Take the infimum over admissible algorithms, followed by the worst case over the instances of this profile. With multiple resources, use this scalar only for an explicitly specified resource projection.



\AtlasInlineMath{x_*}: A global minimizer or quadratic center whose existence is promised by the model \textbf{Domain:} Belongs to the localization domain specified here; used only under the stated existence promise.



The full-space minimizer is unique in the strongly convex class. The center of a positive semidefinite quadratic model need not be unique.



\AtlasInlineMath{A_1}: Accuracy ratio for matched l1 geometry \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{A_1>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{A_1=LR/\varepsilon} when \AtlasInlineMath{B=B_1(0,1)} and \AtlasInlineMath{K=B_1(0,R)}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\alpha_1}: Normalized accuracy for matched l1 geometry \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha_1>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\alpha_1=\varepsilon/(LR)=A_1^{-1}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{M_1}: Saturated dimension-accuracy factor \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{M_1>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{M_1=\min\{d,A_1^2\}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Lambda_1}: Explicit logarithmic scale \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\Lambda_1>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\Lambda_1=\log(ed)+\log(eA_1)} in the small-accuracy domain.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_0^{(1)}}: Fixed small-accuracy endpoint \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c_0^{(1)}\le1/8}.



Fixed independently of varying \AtlasInlineMath{d,L,R,\varepsilon}.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_\diamond}: Fixed normalized threshold for the penalized-support reduction \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{c_\diamond>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{c_\diamond=c_{\rm err}/(8C_{\rm coh})}, where \AtlasInlineMath{c_{\rm err}>0} is the fixed source-error constant and \AtlasInlineMath{C_{\rm coh}>0} is the universal coordinate-coherence constant.



\AtlasInlineMath{\tau_d}: Boundary between the two randomized lower-bound arguments \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\tau_d>0}.



\AtlasInlineMath{\tau_d=c_\diamond/\sqrt{\log(ed)}}.



\AtlasInlineMath{d_1^{(1)}}: Sufficient dimension threshold for the matched l1 joint theorem \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d_1^{(1)}\in\mathbb N}.



A fixed integer large enough for Theorem 1, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1, with \AtlasInlineMath{d_1^{(1)}\ge\max\{3,m_0\}} and \AtlasInlineMath{d^{-1/2}\le\tau_d<c_0^{(1)}} for every \AtlasInlineMath{d\ge d_1^{(1)}}. No numerical threshold is asserted.



\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal L_{\rm img}}: Previously available image-radius lower envelope with its admissibility guards \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal L_{\rm img}\ge0}.




\AtlasMath{\mathcal L_{\rm img}=\sup\left(\{0\}\cup\left\{c_Z\frac{m\min\{m,(Lr_m/\varepsilon)^2\}}{\log(e\min\{m,(Lr_m/\varepsilon)^2\})}:m_0\le m\le d,\ 0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_ZLr_m\right\}\right)}
. An empty set of admissible image dimensions contributes zero.

Let \$a\_B=\textbackslash{}max\_\{\textbackslash{}|u\textbackslash{}|\_2=1\}\textbackslash{}|u\textbackslash{}|\_B\$ and let \$R\_2(K)\$ be a public Euclidean enclosing radius. Then \$\textbackslash{}beta\_2=a\_B\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}beta\$, \$L\_2=a\_BL\$, and \$D\_2=a\_BR\_2(K)\$ give the deterministic smooth envelope
\$\$O\textbackslash{}!\textbackslash{}left(1+\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{d\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}beta D\_2\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\},d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(e+\textbackslash{}beta D\_2\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}right)\$\$
and Lipschitz localization \$O(1+d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(d+1)\textbackslash{}log(e+\allowbreak{}LD\_2/\textbackslash{}varepsilon))\$.

The norm inequality \$\textbackslash{}|v\textbackslash{}|\_B\textbackslash{}le a\_B\textbackslash{}|v\textbackslash{}|\_2\$ and its dual give the stated Euclidean smoothness and Lipschitz constants. Apply the exact\char45{}value Euclidean acceleration or smooth localization theorem with those constants and the public radius; each transformed value remains one scalar call. The global\char45{}minimizer promise is retained for the smooth localization argument.

For a Lipschitz objective minimized over a known convex set \$K\$, define \$g(x)=f(x)+L\_2\textbackslash{}operatorn\allowbreak{}ame\{dist\}\_2(x,K)\$. This is convex and \$2L\_2\$\char45{}Lipschitz, \$\textbackslash{}min g=\textbackslash{}min\_K f\$ on a ball containing \$K\$, and \$f(\textbackslash{}Pi\_Kx)\textbackslash{}le g(x)\$. One value of \$g\$ uses one value of \$f\$ plus public geometry. The Euclidean ball localization theorem therefore returns a legal point of \$K\$ after projection. This is a concrete transfer to a general body, not a presumed general\char45{}body localization theorem.

If \$B=UB\_2(1)\$ and \$K=c+RB\$ for a public invertible matrix \$U\$, set \$g(y)=f(c+Uy)\$. Then \$\textbackslash{}|Uv\textbackslash{}|\_B=\textbackslash{}|v\textbackslash{}|\_2\$ and \$\textbackslash{}|U\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}top w\textbackslash{}|\_2=\textbackslash{}|w\textbackslash{}|\_\{B,*\}\$. Thus both the Lipschitz and smoothness budgets are unchanged, the feasible or localization body becomes \$B\_2(R)\$, and one value plus the inverse output map preserves the exact gap, budget, and guarantee. No condition\char45{}number factor appears. Deterministic acceleration/localization and randomized two\char45{}point methods keep their original algorithm permissions.

For an \$m\$\char45{}dimensional Euclidean image radius \$r\_m(B,K)>0\$, smooth and Lipschitz lower bounds may be maximized over the integers \$m\$ for which their source windows hold.

Define \$r\_m(B,K)\$ as the largest radius of a Euclidean ball contained in \$AK\$, maximized over maps with \$\textbackslash{}|A\textbackslash{}|\_\{B\textbackslash{}to2\}\textbackslash{}le1\$. Dorn et al., Theorem 3.1, gives
\$\$T\textbackslash{}ge\textbackslash{}max\textbackslash{}left\textbackslash{}\{5m/16,\textbackslash{} (m/4096)\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{m,\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}beta r\_m\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\}\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}rig\allowbreak{}ht\textbackslash{}\},\textbackslash{}quad0<\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textbackslash{}\allowbreak{}le\textbackslash{}beta r\_m\textasciicircum{}2/32.\$\$
Theorem 3.3, with its regularization parameter zero, gives
\$\$T\textbackslash{}ge c\_Z\textbackslash{}frac\{m\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{m,(Lr\_m/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}\}\}\{\textbackslash{}log(e\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{m,(Lr\_m/\textbackslash{}varepsilo\allowbreak{}n)\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}\})\},\textbackslash{}quad m\textbackslash{}ge m\_Z\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}circ,\textbackslash{}quad0<\textbackslash{}vareps\allowbreak{}ilon\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_ZLr\_m\allowbreak{}.\$\$
The all\char45{}space nonsmooth transfer uses the source\char39{}s radial penalty for its homogeneous support\char45{}function hard family: a target query is simulated by one bounded source query and known arithmetic, and radial decoding preserves the output comparison. This permits the stronger all\char45{}space target queries without silently importing a bounded\char45{}query lower bound.

For \$B=B\_q\$ and \$K=B\_p(R)\$, put \$\textbackslash{}theta=(1/2\char45{}1/q)\_++(1/p\char45{}1/2)\_+\$ and \$\textbackslash{}gamma=(1/q\char45{}1/p)\_+\$. The source\char39{}s block certificate is
\$\$r\_m\textbackslash{}ge R\textbackslash{}lfloor d/m\textbackslash{}rfloor\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}gamma m\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}\textbackslash{}theta\},\textbackslash{}qquad r\_d=Rd\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}\textbackslash{}theta\}.\$\$
Insert this certificate into each theorem before maximizing over legal \$m\$. For \$q=2\$ and \$p\textbackslash{}le2\$, this is \$r\_m\textbackslash{}ge Rm\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}t\}\$, \$t=1/p\char45{}1/2\$. Other source certificates, such as constant\char45{}radius quotient images, may be added only with their own operator\char45{}norm and dimension conditions. An exact geometric radius does not itself prove a matching optimization upper bound.

The applicable randomized upper bounds are
\$\$O(1+d\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}eta\_\{d,s\}\textbackslash{}\allowbreak{}beta\_2\textbackslash{}Theta\_s/\textbackslash{}varepsil\allowbreak{}on\}),\textbackslash{}quad O(1+d\textbackslash{}eta\_\{d,s\}\textbackslash{}beta\_2\textbackslash{}T\allowbreak{}heta\_s/\textbackslash{}varepsilon),\$\$
\$\$O(1+L\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}Theta\_s d\textasciicircum{}\{1+2/\textbackslash{}min(q,2)\char45{}2/s\}/\textbackslash{}v\allowbreak{}arepsilon\textasciicircum{}2),\textbackslash{}quad O(1+dv\_H L\_2\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}Theta\_H/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2).\$\$

For the smooth directional methods take \$d\textbackslash{}ge8\$, \$1\textbackslash{}le s\textbackslash{}le2\$, \$s\textasciicircum{}*=s/(s\char45{}1)\$, and \$\textbackslash{}eta\_\{d,s\}=\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{s\textasciicircum{}*\char45{}1,16\textbackslash{}log d\char45{}8\textbackslash{}\}d\textasciicircum{}\{2/s\textasciicircum{}*\char45{}1\}\$. Gorbunov, Dvurechensky, and Gasnikov\char39{}s theorems apply to Euclidean smoothness \$\textbackslash{}beta\_2\$ and a prox divergence bounded by \$\textbackslash{}Theta\_s\$. Exact noiseless values use batch size one and two scalar values per direction; a finite positive difference scale can be chosen small enough for the fixed budget.

For the Lipschitz method of Akhavan et al., \$q\$ is the regularity norm and \$s\$ is the prox norm. Their theorem gives expected gap at most \$11.9L\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}Theta\_s d\textasciicircum{}\{1+2/\textbackslash{}min(q,2)\char45{}2/s\}/T\}\$, with two values per round. Tightening the target by a factor three and applying Markov\char39{}s inequality gives success probability \$2/3\$. A usable prox is
\$\$t\_s=\textbackslash{}max\textbackslash{}\{s,1+1/\textbackslash{}log(ed)\textbackslash{}\},\textbackslash{}quad a\_\{s,d\}=\textbackslash{}frac\{d\textasciicircum{}\{2(1/s\char45{}1\allowbreak{}/t\_s)\}\}\{t\_s\char45{}1\},\textbackslash{}quad\textbackslash{}ome\allowbreak{}ga\_s(x)=a\_\{s,d\}\textbackslash{}|x\textbackslash{}|\_\{t\_\allowbreak{}s\}\textasciicircum{}2/2.\$\$
It is 1\char45{}strongly convex in \$\textbackslash{}ell\_s\$ and on \$B\_p(R)\$ has range at most \$a\_\{s,d\}R\textasciicircum{}2d\textasciicircum{}\{2(1/t\_s\char45{}1/p)\_+\}/2\$. In particular, \$q=2\$, \$s=p\textbackslash{}le2\$ gives the advertised \$a\_\{p,d\}d\textasciicircum{}\{2/p\textasciicircum{}*\}(LR/\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\textasciicircum{}2\$ term.

For Shamir\char39{}s general\char45{}prox bound let \$v\_H=(\textbackslash{}mathbb E\textbackslash{}|U\textbackslash{}|\_\{H,*\}\textasciicircum{}4)\textasciicircum{}\{1/2\}\$ for a uniform Euclidean sphere direction. Use ball convolution as the smoothed function, with sphere directions in its gradient estimator. The divergence identity belongs to the ball average; this formulation preserves convexity, Lipschitzness, the \$O(hL\_2)\$ smoothing bias, and the source variance proof. All these witnesses are randomized, even when their value oracle is exact and deterministic.

For \$B=K=B\_1(R)\$, Euclidean conversion gives \$\textbackslash{}beta\_2=d\textbackslash{}beta\$, while the \$\textbackslash{}ell\_1\$ prox and directional factor contribute \$\textbackslash{}Theta\_1=O(R\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(ed))\$ and \$\textbackslash{}eta\_\{d,1\}=O(\textbackslash{}log(ed)/d)\$. Substitution yields \$O(1+d\textbackslash{}log(ed)\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\})\$.

With ball smoothing \$f\_h(x)=\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_\{U\textbackslash{}sim\textbackslash{}operatorname\{Un\allowbreak{}if\}(B\_2)\}f(x+hU)\$ and a sphere direction \$u\$,
\$\$g\_h(x)=\textbackslash{}frac d\{2h\}[F(x+hu;Z)\char45{}F(x\char45{}hu;Z\allowbreak{})]u,\textbackslash{}quad\textbackslash{}mathbb E g\_h=\textbackslash{}nabla f\_h,\textbackslash{}quad\textbackslash{}mathbb E\textbackslash{}|g\_h\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}r\textbackslash{}le(\textbackslash{}sqrt\{2d\}L)\textasciicircum{}r.\$\$
For \$r=2\$, the bound is \$2dL\textasciicircum{}2\$.

For each fixed sample, the scalar difference \$a(u)=F(x+hu;Z)\char45{}F(x\char45{}hu;Z)\$ is odd on the sphere, hence has mean zero, and has Lipschitz constant at most \$2hG\$. Sphere Poincare gives \$\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_u a(u)\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le4h\textasciicircum{}2G\textasciicircum{}2/(d\char45{}1)\$ for \$d\textbackslash{}ge2\$. Thus \$\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_u\textbackslash{}|g\_h\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le d\textasciicircum{}2G\textasciicircum{}2/(d\char45{}1)\textbackslash{}le2dG\textasciicircum{}2\$; for \$d=1\$ the difference quotient is directly bounded by \$G\$. Apply Jensen only to the direction expectation and then integrate over the sample:
\$\$\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_\{Z,u\}\textbackslash{}|g\_h\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}r\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_Z(\textbackslash{}mathbb E\_u\textbackslash{}|g\_h\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2)\textasciicircum{}\{r/2\}\textbackslash{}le(2d)\textasciicircum{}\{r/2\}\textbackslash{}mathbb E G\textasciicircum{}r.\$\$
No second moment of \$G\$ is needed when \$r<2\$. The divergence theorem for ball convolution gives the unbiasedness identity. Integrability follows from the Lipschitz difference bound. Convexity gives \$f\_h\textbackslash{}ge f\$, and \$|f\_h\char45{}f|\textbackslash{}le hL\$; mean strong convexity is preserved on the region where every translated point satisfies it. All statements hold conditionally on the past when the next sample and direction are fresh. Reusing an old adaptively explored sample does not automatically preserve this conditional moment calculation.

For a \$\textbackslash{}mu\$\char45{}strongly\char45{}convex mean with \$\textbackslash{}mathbb E G\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le L\textasciicircum{}2\$, \$K\$ rounds and \$T=2K\$ scalar calls give
\$\$\textbackslash{}mathbb E[f(\textbackslash{}bar x\_K)\char45{}f\_*]\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}frac\{4dL\textasciicircum{}2\}\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}mu(K+1)\}+2hL.\$\$
The merely convex branch uses \$O(d(LR/\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\textasciicircum{}2)\$ values.

Run the paired estimator on \$K\_h=B\_2(R\char45{}h)\$ and let \$x\_\{h,*\}\$ minimize \$f\_h\$ there. The shrinkage comparator \$y=(1\char45{}h/R)x\_*\$ gives \$f\_h(y)\textbackslash{}le f\_*+2hL\$. Set \$V=2dL\textasciicircum{}2\$, \$\textbackslash{}eta\_t=2/[\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)]\$, and \$D\_t=\textbackslash{}mathbb E\textbackslash{}|x\_t\char45{}x\_\{h,*\}\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\$. Projection and strong convexity yield
\$\$\textbackslash{}mathbb E[f\_h(x\_t)\char45{}f\_h(x\_\{h,*\})]\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}mu(t\char45{}1)\}4D\_t\char45{}\textbackslash{}\allowbreak{}frac\{\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)\}4D\_\{t+1\}+\textbackslash{}\allowbreak{}frac\{V\}\{\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)\}.\$\$
Multiply by \$t\$, telescope, and average with weights \$2t/[K(K+1)]\$. The initial distance coefficient is zero and the last is nonpositive, giving \$2V/[\textbackslash{}mu(K+1)]\$. Add the comparator error. For expected accuracy choose, for example, \$h=\textbackslash{}varepsilon/(8L)\$ and \$K+1\textbackslash{}ge8dL\textasciicircum{}2/(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$. For success probability \$2/3\$, use \$h=\textbackslash{}varepsilon/(12L)\$ and \$K+1\textbackslash{}ge24dL\textasciicircum{}2/(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$, making the expected nonnegative gap at most \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon/3\$ before Markov.

For convex objectives, the projected averaging recursion with step \$R/\textbackslash{}sqrt\{VK\}\$ gives expected optimization error at most \$R\textbackslash{}sqrt\{V/K\}\$, plus the same smoothing/shrinkage error. Uniform component sampling makes the estimator unbiased for the finite\char45{}sum mean and costs exactly two selected\char45{}component values per round. Neither the oracle nor the components need be stochastic in that case; the algorithm supplies the randomness. These bounds also hold under an almost\char45{}sure Lipschitz promise, since it implies the required second moment. The Gaussian lower construction in the separate lower lemma does not acquire that stronger promise.

Retained premises: the frozen common specification gives global L\char45{}Lipschitzness in the B norm, known B,K, output in K, and charges scalar objective values. Both views permit deterministic algorithms; randomized g1 requires success at least 2/3. The q1 quantities minimize a nonnegative call budget. For u\ensuremath{\in}K=c\_K+\ensuremath{\rho}B, ||u\char45{}c\_K||\_B\ensuremath{\le}\ensuremath{\rho}, hence f(c\_K)\char45{}f(u)\ensuremath{\le}L\ensuremath{\rho}. Taking the infimum over u proves gap\ensuremath{\le}L\ensuremath{\rho}. Returning the known center without objective information therefore succeeds deterministically whenever \ensuremath{\varepsilon}\ensuremath{\ge}L\ensuremath{\rho}, including equality. If \ensuremath{\rho}=0, K is a singleton and the gap is zero. Nonnegative costs give C*\ensuremath{\ge}0, proving C*=0 in both views. No global\char45{}minimizer promise or extra oracle is used. Sharpness for \ensuremath{\rho}>0: choose a nonzero vector a and normalize it by max\_\{b\ensuremath{\in}B\}a·b, positive by compactness, symmetry and nonempty interior. Then max\_\{b\ensuremath{\in}B\}a·b=1 and |a·v|\ensuremath{\le}||v||\_B by the gauge definition. The global convex functions f\_±(x)=±La·(x\char45{}c\_K) are admissible and have minimum \char45{}L\ensuremath{\rho} on K. Their \ensuremath{\varepsilon}\char45{}good sets respectively require a·(x\char45{}c\_K)\ensuremath{\le}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}/L\char45{}\ensuremath{\rho} and a·(x\char45{}c\_K)\ensuremath{\ge}\ensuremath{\rho}\char45{}\ensuremath{\varepsilon}/L. These sets are disjoint for \ensuremath{\varepsilon}<L\ensuremath{\rho}. A zero\char45{}call algorithm has the same output distribution on both objectives, so one success probability is at most 1/2. It cannot satisfy deterministic g1 or randomized success 2/3. This last argument proves only nontriviality below the endpoint, not a main\char45{}rate lower bound.

For \$g(z)=f(Rz)/(LR)\$, convexity and global l1 Lipschitzness give \$|g(z)\char45{}g(w)|\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}|z\char45{}w\textbackslash{}|\_1\$. A value of \$g\$ is computed by one value of \$f\$, and \$z\textbackslash{}in B\_1(1)\$ decodes to \$Rz\textbackslash{}in K\$ with the same normalized gap \$\textbackslash{}alpha\_1\$. This preserves every pathwise budget and the per\char45{}instance seed probability.

Lemma 1 of Colombo\_KIMI\_001 uses exactly \$2\textbackslash{}lceil576dA\_1\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(2d)\textbackslash{}rceil\$ scalar queries and yields expected feasible error at most \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon/3\$. Nonnegativity of the gap and Markov\char39{}s inequality give success probability at least \$2/3\$. Its witness is randomized. The public\char45{}body value\char45{}only theorem in Lemma 2 instead gives a deterministic witness with \$O(d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(d+1)\textbackslash{}log(4A\_1))\$ calls; the cited Protasov ingredient is for an explicit known body, with free auxiliary geometric computation.

For the source lower bound, ZZQL Theorem 5 applies to a fixed distribution of max\char45{}support objectives. Its original Lipschitz constant is 2; divide the functions and their errors by 2. The resulting rows are truncated Gaussian vectors divided by \$2\textbackslash{}sqrt d\$. Their coordinate\char45{}coherence event has constant probability uniformly over the legal numbers of rows. Colombo\_KIMI\_001 Theorem 2 uses the known penalty \$\textbackslash{}lambda\textbackslash{}operatorname\{di\allowbreak{}st\}\_1(x,B\_2(d\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}1/2\}))\$, with \$\textbackslash{}lambda=C\_\{\textbackslash{}rm coh\}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}log(ed)\}\$. Its decoder sends every feasible output to that inner ball; positive homogeneity answers every finite full\char45{}space target query with at most one feasible Euclidean source query. Conditioning costs only the fixed prior probability. Thus its lower bound retains the same all\char45{}space oracle, arbitrary output and unrestricted randomized algorithm scope.

Set \$M\_1=\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{d,A\_1\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}\}\$. For \$\textbackslash{}alpha\_1\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}tau\_d\$, Theorem 2 yields \$c dM\_1/[\textbackslash{}log(ed)\textbackslash{}log(eM\_1)]\$. Above \$\textbackslash{}tau\_d\$, Corollary 1 gives \$d/[16384\textbackslash{}log(ed)]\$. There \$A\_1\textasciicircum{}2<\textbackslash{}log(ed)/c\_\textbackslash{}diamond\textasciicircum{}2\$, so the ratio of the two\char45{}point upper to the latter lower is \$O(A\_1\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log\textasciicircum{}2(ed))=O(\textbackslash{}log\textasciicircum{}3(ed))\$ for fixed source constants. For \$\textbackslash{}alpha\_1\textbackslash{}le d\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}1/2\}\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}tau\_d\$, \$M\_1=d\$ and the regional lower is \$\textbackslash{}Omega(d\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}log\textasciicircum{}2(ed))\$, independent of any further accuracy refinement. Theorem 1 also gives the weaker but uniform expression \$a dM\_1/\textbackslash{}Lambda\_1\textasciicircum{}2\$ over the complete stated small\char45{}accuracy domain.

Every admissible image\char45{}radius lower inequality remains valid. Taking its supremum with zero gives \$\textbackslash{}mathcal L\_\{\textbackslash{}rm img\}\$, and taking its maximum with the new applicable lower cannot weaken the bracket. In particular, a previously available finer\char45{}accuracy image lower is not discarded. The upper envelope is the minimum of applicable algorithms under the same guarantee. On the fixed\char45{}\$c\$ slice \$\textbackslash{}alpha\_1=c/\textbackslash{}sqrt d\$, with \$c>0\$ fixed, \$dM\_1=d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{1,c\textasciicircum{}\{\char45{}2\}\textbackslash{}\}\$ and \$\textbackslash{}Lambda\_1=O\_c(\textbackslash{}log(ed))\$, giving a new \$\textbackslash{}Omega\_c(d\textasciicircum{}2/\textbackslash{}log\textasciicircum{}2(ed))\$ lower while retaining the existing \$O\_c(d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(ed))\$ randomized upper.

A lower bound for all randomized algorithms also holds for deterministic algorithms. The deterministic upper is only the deterministic known\char45{}body method; the randomized two\char45{}point witness is not used in that view. Consequently the deterministic fine\char45{}accuracy region is near optimal, whereas its coarse\char45{}accuracy bracket retains the explicitly displayed polynomial factor.
